RESUMO

O tratamento endodôntico visa reduzir ao máximo a carga microbiana presente no
sistema de canais radiculares por meio do preparo químico -mecânico, utilizando
instrumentos manuais e/ou mecanizados sob ação de substâncias irrigadoras. Para evitar
o fracasso do tratamento endodôntico, é importante selar adequadamente os canais após
o preparo químico -mecânico, a fim de evitar microinfiltração microbiana. O selamento
envolve o uso de guta -percha e cimento endodôntico, este último aderindo à dentina e
preenchendo os espaços entre a guta-percha e o sistema de canais radiculares, entretanto
falhas na integridade e limitações dos materiais obturadores e restauradores podem
predispor a microinfiltração. Com o objetivo de se entender melhor a microinfiltração,
estudos laboratoriais apresentam diversos tipos de análise em materiais obturadores. Entre
os modelos, destaca -se o método de duas câmaras para avaliar a infiltração microbiana,
contudo não garante que esta microinfiltração ocorre através do espaço do canal radicular
e não por outras vias. O objetivo deste estudo foi desenvolver um protocolo laboratorial para
avaliar a microinfiltração microbiana através dos cimentos endodônticos, de forma a garantir
a visualização da via de infiltração do inóculo. Para tanto, foi desenvolvido um sistema
contendo raízes de dentes bovinos, tubos de vidro com pérolas de vidro e meio de cultura
ágar bile esculina. Cada raiz, após preparo, desinfecção e ester ilização em autoclave, foi
inserida em um tubo estéril de vidro contendo pérolas de vidro, previamente pesadas, este
conjunto foi parcialmente preenchido com meio ágar bile esculina e sua esterilidade
verificada pela incubação por 24 h. Após este período, o sistema foi inoculado com
Enterococcus faecalis ATCC 29212, incubado a 36°C e observado por 6 semanas. O ensaio
laboratorial proposto permitiu detectar se a infiltração por E. faecalis ocorreu via canal
radicular ou externamente a raiz devido a alteração da coloração por oxidação do meio de
cultura; na região apical através do seu longo eixo do canal radicular ou superficialmente
ao meio de cultura quando, por falha do operador, alguma quantidade do inóculo seja
depositado externamente à raiz. Conclui -se que este novo protocolo apresenta as
características necessárias para avaliar microinfiltração microbiana através dos cimentos
endodônticos, visto sua capacidade de demonstrar a via da microinfiltração, garantindo
diferenciar microinfiltração de contaminação.

Palavras-chave: bactéria; microbiologia; endodontia; infiltração dentária; protocolo.

ABSTRACT

Endodontic treatment aims to reduce as much as possible the microbial load present in the
root canal system through chemical -mechanical preparation, using manual and/or
mechanized instruments under the action of irrigating substances. To avoid the failure of
endodontic treatment, it is important to adequately seal the canals after chemical -
mechanical preparation, to prevent microbial microleakage. The sealing involves the use of
gutta-percha and endodontic cement, the latter adhering to dentin and filling t he spaces
between the gutta-percha and the dentin walls; however, failures in integrity and limitations
of obturating and restorative materials may predispose to microleakage. With the objective
of better understanding microleakage, laboratory studies pres ent several types of analysis
in obturating materials. Among the models, the two -chamber method stands out for
evaluating microbial leakage; however, it does not guarantee that this microleakage occurs
through the root canal space and not by other pathways. The objective of this study was to
develop a laboratory protocol to evaluate microbial microleakage through endodontic
sealers, in order to ensure visualization of the inoculum leakage pathway. For this purpose,
a system was developed containing bovine tooth roots, glass tubes with glass beads, and
bile esculin agar culture medium. Each root, after preparation, disinfection, and sterilization
in autoclave, was inserted into a sterile glass tube containing previously weighed glass
beads; this set was partially filled with bile esculin agar medium and its sterility verified by
incubation for 24 h. After this period, the system was inoculated with Enterococcus faecalis
ATCC 29212, incubated at 36°C, and observed for 6 weeks. The proposed laboratory assay
allowed detection of whether infiltration by E. faecalis occurred via the root canal or
externally to the root due to color change by oxidation of the culture medium; in the apical
region through the long axis of the root canal or superficially to the culture medium when,
due to operator failure, some amount of the inoculum was deposited externally to the root.
It is concluded that thi s new protocol presents the necessary characteristics to evaluate
microbial microleakage through endodontic cements, given its ability to demonstrate the
pathway of microleakage, ensuring differentiation between microleakage and
contamination.

Keywords: bacteria; microbiology; endodontics; dental leakage; protocol.

1 INTRODUÇÃO


A perda da integridade das estruturas dentárias favorece a penetração de
microrganismos no sistema de canais radiculares (SCR). Esse evento ocorre quando
estruturas dentárias, como o esmalte ou cemento, que compõem a parte externa do dente,
e a dentina, que representa a maior parte da estrutura dentária, sofrem ruptura por fatores
biológicos ou traumáticos (Farci; Soni, 2023). O estudo clássico de Kakehashi , Stanley e
Fitzgerald (1965), demonstrou que a presença de microrganismos é determinante para o
desenvolvimento de lesões periapicais, o que foi corroborado por estudos mais recentes
(Aw, 2016; Farci; Soni, 2023; Nair, 2004).
Dentre os microrganismos frequentemente associados à infecção endodôntica
destacam-se Enterococcus faecalis e Candida albicans (Ajmi et al., 2024), que possuem a
capacidade de formar biofilmes, conferindo -lhes resistência aos processos de limpeza do
SCR, elevando o risco de falha no tratamento endodôntico (Siqueira Jr; Rôças, 2008).
Particularmente, E. faecalis destaca-se por sua resistência aos antimicrobianos
convencionais e pela habilidade de sobreviver em condições desfavoráveis dentro do SCR
(Sharma et al., 2025). A complexa estrutura dos canais radiculares, incluindo istmos e
canais laterais, se tornam nichos para a sobrevivência microbiana, dificultando a limpeza
química e mecânica (Ajmi et al., 2024; Martins et al., 2019; Prada et al., 2019; Sharma et
al., 2025; Siqueira Jr; Rôças, 2008).
Nesse contexto, o tratamento endodôntico visa reduzir ao máximo a carga
microbiana presente no SCR por meio do preparo químico -mecânico (PQM), utilizando
instrumentos manuais e/ou mecanizados sob ação de substâncias irrigadoras, como
hipoclorito de sódio ( Haapasalo et al., 2010), e obturação com materiais biocompatíveis
(Gatelli; Bortolini, 2014; Macedo et al., 2021; Schilder, 2006; Vier et al., 2011).
A guta-percha, que atua como material obturador, apresenta ação limitada, e não é
capaz, isoladamente, de garantir um selamento duradouro (Schilder, 2006). Dessa forma,
a utilização de cimentos endodônticos, pode contribuir para a melhora desse selamento
(Komabayashi et al., 2020; Kowalski et al., 2024). Sendo assim, a guta -percha associada
aos cimentos endodônticos buscam preencher de forma tridimensional o SCR, auxiliando
na prevenção de futuras infecções (Hori et al., 2021; Siqueira Jr.; Roças; 2008).

12


Evitar a microinfiltração microbiana, através da obturação, é essencial para
aumentar a eficácia, a previsibilidade e o sucesso dos procedimentos endodônticos (Ajmi
et al., 2024; Jafari et al., 2017). Contudo, falhas na integridade e limitações dos materiais
obturadores e restauradores podem resultar em microinfiltração (Ajmi et al., 2024; Jafari;
Jafari, 2017; Wuersching et al., 2023).
Para que sejam considerados ideais, os cimentos endodônticos devem reunir
propriedades que garantam excelente selamento e compatibilidade biológica com os
tecidos periapicais (Rekha et al., 2023). Esses cimentos podem apresentar características
como: biocompatibilidade, selamento eficaz, ação antimicrobiana, estabilidade em meio
úmido, radiopacidade, boa adesão ao canal radicular, tempo de trabalho prolongado e
ausência de contração durante a presa (Bran stetter; Von Fraunhofer, 1982), e podem
apresentar em sua composição: óxido de zinco -eugenol, salicilato, óxido de zinco -ácido
graxo, ionômero de vidro, silicone, resina epóxi, silicato tricálcico (agregado de trióxido
mineral MTA/biocerâmica) e resina de metacrilato (Komabayashi et al., 2020).
Ainda que sejam encontrados cimentos endodônticos com as propriedades
descritas anteriormente, tem -se observado o insucesso dos tratamentos endodônticos
devido à microinfiltração microbiana, resultando em uma infecção endodôntica secundária
(D'costa; Bangera; Kutty, 2017; Khayat; Lee; Torabinejad, 1993; Roghanizad; Jones, 1996;
Swanson; Madison, 1987).
É importante realizar pesquisas laboratoriais que verifiquem a microinfiltração
através dos cimentos endodônticos já utilizados, bem como também de novos (Akhavan et
al., 2011; Jafari; Jafari, 2017; Jafari et al ., 2017). Assim sendo, estudos apresentam
diferentes metodologias para verificar a microinfiltração, como, por infiltração de glicose,
com corantes como o azul de metileno, por pressão de fluidos no corpo de prova (calculado
a partir do movimento da bolha) e também microinfiltração bacteriana; com o intuito de
qualificar o selamento dos condutos radiculares (Akhavan et al., 2011; Jafari; Jafari, 2017;
Jafari et al., 2017). Dentre os modelos para verificar microinfiltração microbiana, destaca -
se o método que utiliza um sistema de duas câmaras. A câmara superior é composta por
um microtubo adaptado, contendo raízes dentárias previamente preparadas e seladas com
esmalte de unha e cianoacrilato. Após esterilização com óxido de etileno, essa câmera é
acoplada à inferior (um frasco de vidro contendo meio de cultura líquido estéril). A
extremidade da raiz permanece submersa no meio, sem tocar o fundo do frasco. A turvação

13


do meio de cultura indica ocorrência de microinfiltração bacteriana (Mansour et al., 2024;
Shahi et al., 2017; Yanpiset et al., 2018).
No entanto, revisões de literatura apontam limitações nos estudos de
microinfiltração microbiana com duas câmaras (Jafari; Jafari, 2017; Rechenberg; De-Deus;
Zehnder, 2011), como o uso do cianoacrilato como material selante, onde a microinfiltração
pode ocorrer na interface dente -tubo da câmara superior e não pelo espaço do canal
radicular (Jafari et al., 2017).
Embora muitos dos estudos que avaliaram microinfiltração tenham utilizado dentes
humanos (Jafari et al., 2017; Jafari; Jafari, 2017; Kim et al., 2015; Komabayashi et al., 2020;
Moradi et al., 2009; Rechenberg; De-Deus; Zehnder, 2011; Rekha et al., 2023; Wuersching
et al., 2023), a substituição por dentes bovinos em estudos de endodontia tem se mostrado
eficaz (Azevedo et al., 2025; Brackett et al., 1998; Carvalho et al., 2018; Schmalz et al.,
2001; Silva et al., 2019; Yassen; Platt; Hara, 2011). Mesmo con siderando que a dentina
bovina apresenta maior permeabilidade, essa diferença é pequena, uma vez que o número
e diâmetro de túbulos são semelhantes às da dentina humana, porém com maior densidade
(Schilke et al., 2000), sendo os dentes bovinos considerados uma alternativa viável para
testes de permeabilidade e resistência de união em obturação com guta -percha e cimento
(Carvalho et al., 2018; Silva et al., 2019). Adicionalmente, a utilização desses dentes em
ensaios laboratoriais apresenta como vantagem a m aior facilidade de obtenção em
comparação aos dentes humanos (Schmalz et al., 2001), cuja disponibilidade é limitada
(Tanaka et al., 2008).
Uma vez que o selamento eficaz do SCR está associado ao sucesso do tratamento
endodôntico e os métodos de avaliação da microinfiltração microbiana são questionados
por não garantirem que a via de acesso do microrganismo ao meio de cultura ocorreu
através da obturação, t orna-se importante o desenvolvimento de um novo modelo
experimental que permita avaliar com precisão a infiltração microbiana em raízes obturadas
com diferentes materiais obturadores.

ABSTRACT:
To avoid failure of endodontic treatment, it is important to properly seal the canals after chemomechanical preparation, in o rder to
avoid microleakage. Typically, sealing involves the use of gutta-percha and sealing cement, the latter of which adheres to the dentin
and fills the spaces between the gutta-percha and the dentin walls. Laboratory studies have been performed to detect microleakage
of endodontic sealers based on various criteria, including microbiological ones, however none guarantee that the le akage occurred
through the root canal space and not through other pathways. Our protocols propose a new laboratory assay to evaluate bacteri al
microleakage in endodontic sealers, ensuring visualization of the correct inoculum infiltration pathway. Furthermore, we present the
main critical parameters and provide suggestions on how to manage them. These protocols allow the detection of bacterial
microleakage in bovine teeth filled with endodontic sealer and inoculated with Enterococcus faecalis.

INTRODUCTION:
The tooth has two main parts, crown and root, being externally covered by enamel and cement, respectively. Internally, it
is composed of dentin and dental pulp ( Farci & Soni, 2023 ). Endodontic infection occurs mainly due to the exposure of the dental
pulp to the oral cavity (Nair, 2004), and the presence of microorganisms in the root canal system triggers an inflammatory response
resulting in apical periodontitis (Aw, 2016; Kakerashi et al., 1965; Nair, 2004 ).
The success of endodontic treatment in teeth with apical periodontitis is associated with reducing the bacterial load to
levels compatible with healing ( Siqueria & Roças, 2008 ). This treatment relies on a chemomechanical approach, which combines
instrumentation and irrigation procedures for achieving effective cleansing of the root canal system ( Byström et al., 1987; Garcez et
al., 2007). To avoid endodontic treatment failure it is also important to properly seal the canals after chemomechanical preparation,
in order to prevent microleakage (Deshpande & Naik, 2015; Jafari & Jafari, 2017, Komabayashi et al., 2020; Muliyar et al., 2014,).

17


Typically, sealing involves the use of gutta-percha, a semi-solid material, and sealing cement. Gutta-percha acts as a filling
material, while endodontic cement adheres to the dentin and fills spaces between gutta -percha and the dentinal walls ( Muliyar et
al., 2014).
Endodontic sealers are classified by composition as: zinc oxide -eugenol, salicylate, zinc oxide -fatty acid, glass ionomer,
silicone, epoxy resin, tricalcium silicate ( MTA Mineral Trioxide Aggregate /bioceramic), and methacrylate resin ( Komabayashi et al.,
2020). Currently, different laboratory studies have been performed for detecting microleakage of endodontic sealers, based on: dye
penetration, dye extraction, fluid filtration, glucose penetration, bacterial leakage, endotoxin infiltration, caffeine pene tration,
caffeine microleakage, protein penetration, copper ion diffusion, radioisotope penetration, and electrochemical leakage tests (Jafari
& Jafari, 2017; Komabayashi et al ., 2020 ). Review studies have presented limitations and disadvantages associated with these
methodologies (Jafari & Jafari 2017; Rechenberg et al., 2010; Verissimo & Do Vale, 2006 ), especially regarding microbial leakage in
two-chamber models. The main limitation they report is that this model does not guarantee that the leakage actually occurred
through the root canal space pathways and not through other pathways (Rechenberg et al., 2010).
Our study brings a novel laboratory assay to evaluate the bacterial microleakage of endodontic sealers ( Fig. 1), ensuring
visualization of the correct inoculum leakage pathway. This will allow identification of whether or not the leakage is occurring through
the root canal space. We describe the selection and cleaning of bovine teeth in basic protocol 1. Basic protocol 2 presents the inclusion
criteria and storage of the teeth. Once teeth are included, the decoronation process and standardization of shape and size of the root
canals are described in basic protocol 3, whereas basic protocol 4 provides the preparatio n of a set containing the tooth to be
inoculated. The inoculum preparation and the set inoculation with Enterococcus faecalis are described in basic protocol 5 and 6,
respectively. Basic protocol 7 demonstrates how to incubate and maintain the sets throughout all 6 weeks of experiment.

CAUTIONS
CAUTION: E. faecalis is a Biosafety Level 2 [BSL-2] pathogen. Follow all appropriate guidelines and regulations for the use
and handling of pathogenic microorganisms.
CAUTION: The use of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), like gloves, face shield and mask, during all protocols is essential
to avoid contamination of the operator and the sample.

18


CAUTION: Microbiological steps should be performed in an aseptic environment such as a biosafety cabinet (according to
the manufacturer's instructions) or working area of the bunsen burner to avoid contamination.
CAUTION: Dental procedures should be performed by a specialist in the field. It is important to highlight that procedures
involving root canals must be performed by a specialist in endodontics.
CAUTION: Microbiological procedures must be performed by a microbiological specialist.

STRATEGIC PLANNING
Obtaining the number of samples of freshly extracted bovine teeth (basic protocol 1) must be carefully planned prior to the
experiment. This will depend on previous contact with a slaughterhouse, so that they can plan and reserve the number of teeth
requested.
BASIC PROTOCOL 1
Basic protocol title:
BOVINE TEETH SELECTION AND CLEANING
Introductory paragraph:
This protocol describes a method to select bovine teeth by visual inspection and then clean them using a periodontal
curette. It is important to use PPE to protect the operator from contamination. This protocol allows the selection of clean
bovine teeth with completely formed roots and root size of at least 22 mm.

Fresh bovine teeth
0.9% sterile saline (see recipe)

Gloves
Ruler
Face shield
Periodontal Gracey curette (Golgran-Millennium, São Caetano do Sul, SP, Brazil)
Plastic flasks with lid
Refrigerator

Visual evaluation
1. Obtain fresh bovine teeth from a slaughterhouse after the animal has been slaughtered (a routine activity in the
commercialization of meat for nutritional purposes).

The Brazilian Council for the Control of Animal Experimentation, as well as IACUC (Institutional Animal Care and Use
Committee), only evaluate the use of live animals in research or animals that have been euthanized for research purposes,
which was not the case in this protocol, so ethical approval is not applicable in this case.

2. Wear gloves to avoid contamination.

Fresh bovine teeth routinely come with biological materials, such as bone and gum debris, hence the need for protection with

3. Perform visual inspection.

Cleaning

BASIC PROTOCOL 3
Basic protocol title:
TOOTH STANDARDIZATION
Introductory paragraph:
In order to obtain a standardized and clean sample of bovine roots, basic protocol 3 describes the decoronation process as
well as the standardization regarding shape and size of the root canals, the isolation of the external root face and

22


sterilization of the root samples. It is important to use PPE to avoid debris injuring the face during decoronation and root
canal preparation.

2.5% sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl)
17% ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) (Lysanda Dental Products Ltd)

Double sided diamond cutting disc (Microdont, Socorro, SP, Brazil)

Endodontic Ruler
Permanent marker

K-file #15 (Dentsply Sirona)
Largo drill #3 (Dentsply Sirona)
Largo drill #4 (Dentsply Sirona)
Largo drill #5 (Dentsply Sirona)
Electric motor with contra-angle VDW Silver Reciproc® (Dentsply Sirona)

W File #25.07 mechanized reciprocating files (TDK)
W File #35.06 mechanized reciprocating files(TDK)
W File #45.05 mechanized reciprocating files (TDK)

Bovine tooth decoronation
1. Wear PPE to avoid accidents and contamination.

It is important to use PPE (lab coat, face shield, mask and gloves) at this stage due to the formation of dentin dust during
decoronation, which can lead to eye irritation and airway dryness.

2. Connect the double sided diamond (Microdont) cutting disc on the mandrel (Microdont) clamping device and attach them
to the straight handpiece of the dental laboratory electric motor (Metalurgica FAVA Industria e Comercio).

3. Cut the crown of each tooth 2-3 mm below the cemento-enamel junction.

Standardization of the bovine root’s cervical third

4. Standardize all roots with 22 mm.

Use an endodontic ruler and a permanent marker to trace a 22 mm distance from the apical region to the cervical region of
each root.

5. Insert the bovine tooth in the bench vise and fill it with 10 mL of sodium hypochlorite 2.5%, using a syringe with needle.

6. Introduce the #10 file(Dentsply Sirona) into the root canal with oscillatory and passive cyclic motions (clockwise to fit the
canal wall and counterclockwise to cut with controlled pressure).

During this process, irrigate the canal with 2.5% sodium hypochlorite using the 10 mL syringe with the needle attached, before
and between each cycle to remove debris until #10(Dentsply Sirona) file reaches the apex (working length).

7. Repeat exactly the same kinematics presented in step 6 with the #15 file.

23


8. Connect the #3 Largo ( Dentsply Sirona) drill on the oscillating contra -angle of the VDW Silver Reciproc® electric
motor(Dentsply Sirona).

9. Enlarge the cervical preflaring of the root with the #3 Largo drills (Dentsply Sirona) in continuous rotation at 1000 rpm.

Insert only the active part of the Largo drill(Dentsply Sirona) in the canal.

10. Repeat steps 8 and 9 with a #4 Largo drill(Dentsply Sirona)

11. Repeat steps 8 and 9 with a #5 Largo dril(Dentsply Sirona)l.

Standardization of the bovine root’s third medium apex

12. Connect the #20.07 W file ( TDK) on the oscillating contra -angle of the VDW Silver Reciproc® electric motor( Dentsply
Sirona).

13. Gently, introduce the file into the root canal, advancing apically with a pecking motion (descending and ascending motion)
in sets of three pecks. Repeat this step until you reach the apex.

During this process, irrigate the channel with 2.5% sodium hypochlorite before and between each set of three pecks to remove
debris. After each set of three pecks, remove the instrument from the root canal and clean the file.

14. Repeat steps 12 and 13 with W File #25.07 (TDK) mechanized reciprocating files.

15. Repeat steps 12 and 13 with W File #35.06 (TDK) mechanized reciprocating files.

16. Repeat steps 12 and 13 with W File #45.05 (TDK) mechanized reciprocating files.

Cleansing of the bovine root canal

17. Close the apex of the root, temporarily, using the smallest possible amount of utility wax (Lysanda Dental Products Ltd).

This step allows the irrigating substances to remain in the canal during the cleansing process.

18. Fill a 10 mL syringe with 17% EDTA (Lysanda Dental Products Ltd) and another 10 mL syringe with 2.5% NaOCl.

19. Gently irrigate the bovine root canal with 2 mL of 17% EDTA (Lysanda Dental Products Ltd).

20. Use the Easy Clean instrument (B assi Equipamentos), attached to the contra -angle of the VDW Silver ® reciprocating
motor(Dentsply Sirona), in continuous rotation at 1000 rpm for 20 seconds in order to activate the EDTA ( Lysanda Dental
Products Ltd).

21. Gently irrigate the bovine root canal with 2 mL of 2.5% NaOCl.

22. Use the Easy Clean instrument, attached to the contra-angle of the VDW Silver ® reciprocating motor(Dentsply Sirona), in
continuous rotation at 1000 rpm for 20 seconds in order to activate the NaOCl.

23. Repeat steps 19 through 22 two more times.

Steps 5 to 23 comprise the endodontic chemomechanical preparation.

Sealing and sterilizing the bovine teeth

24. After cleaning the bovine root canals, leave them at room temperature for 24h.

It is important to wait 24 hours so that the bovine rennet can dry completely.

25. Apply two coats of nail polish to all root surfaces except the apex and on the coronal plane. Wait 24 h between each
application of nail polish.

This step allows us to isolate possible cracks and side channels on the external root that were not previously observed.

24


26. Twenty-four hours after drying the second layer of enamel, sterilize the bovine roots by autoclaving using a surgical grade
pack for each root.

BASIC PROTOCOL 4
Basic protocol title:
SET PREPARATION
Introductory paragraph:
Basic protocol 4 describes the method for obtaining sterile sets composed of: glass pearls, a bovine root filled with the test
endodontic sealer and solid culture medium in a glass tube with a lid. It is important to use aseptic techniques to avoid any
contamination of the set. Although this protocol does not describe the process of obturation with endodontic sealers, we
strongly recommend that this process be performed strictly following the manufacturer's instructions and using aseptic
techniques in an aseptic environment.

70% ethanol
Bile aesculin agar (see recipe), 55° to 60°C

Glass pearls (3 mm)
Analytical balance
5 mL borosilicate glass tube (16 x 41 mm) with lid
Surgical grade paper
Surgical grade sealer
Autoclave
100 mL borosilicate glass flask with lid
Water bath
Tweezers
Bunsen burner or biosafety cabinet
Sterile tips
Micropipette
PPE
Bacteriological incubator

1. Weigh 3.5 g of glass pearls

2. In a 5 mL borosilicate glass tube with lid (Fig. 4a), insert the 3.5 g of glass pearls (Fig. 4b).

3. Autoclave (121°C/20 min) these tubes with glass pearls.

4. After autoclaving the bile aesculin agar medium in the 100 mL borosilicate glass flask with lid, keep this medium in a water
bath previously set to 60°C.

The water bath is important to keep the bile aesculin agar medium between 55° to 60°C, allowing the medium to remain in
the liquid state after the autoclaving process.

5. Perform the root obturation with the endodontic sealer being tested, strictly following the manufacturer's instructions.

After obturation remove the excess endodontic sealer, using a # 4 largo drill, keeping 3 mm of obturation. The smear layer
should be removed with 17% EDTA under agitation. Perform step 5 using aseptic techniques in an aseptic environment.

6. Insert aseptically, using sterilized tweezers, each root (immediately after root canal obturation with the test sealer) within
the glass pearls 5 mm short of the bottom of the 5 mL glass tube (Fig 4c).

Make sure the tubes with glass pearls are completely dry before performing step 5.

This insertion needs to be performed with the sterile tip (previously attached in the micropipettor) leaning against the internal
wall of the 5 mL tube to avoid touching the root (Fig 4d). Do not move the tube until the medium solidifies.

25



To avoid contamination, steps 5 and 6 need to be performed using aseptic techniques (wear PPE and disinfect gloves and
surfaces with 70% ethanol) in an aseptic environment such as biosafety cabinet, laminar flow hood or working area of the
bunsen burner.

8. Set the bacteriological incubator to 36 °C and incubate the sets (tubes containing root, glass pearls and medium) 24 h before

BASIC PROTOCOL 5
Basic protocol title:
INOCULUM PREPARATION
Introductory paragraph:
This protocol describes how to obtain an inoculum with 10 9 Colony Forming Units (CFU)/mL of E. faecalis American Type
Culture Collection (ATCC) 29212, from a frozen glycerol stock, in Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) broth. To avoid contamination
rigorous aseptic techniques are necessary in all steps of basic protocol 5. For example, perform all steps wearing PPE in an
aseptic environment such as a biosafety cabinet or working area of the bunsen burner, and disinfect gloves and surfaces
with 70% ethanol.
Materials:
E. faecalis ATCC 29212 frozen stock in BHI broth with glycerol (at final concentration of 20% vol./vol. glycerol)
BHI agar (see recipe)
BHI broth (see recipe)
70% ethanol

PPE
Bunsen burner or biosafety cabinet
Sterile inoculation loop.
Bacteriological incubator
13 x 100 mm glass tubes
Spectrophotometer (Marca)

1. Using aseptic technique remove a small chunk of frozen E. faecalis from the cryotube, using a sterile inoculating loop.

2. Streak E. faecalis onto the BHI agar plate.

Starting from the edge of the Petri dish, in the first quadrant using the sterile inoculation loop streak the small chunk of E.
faecalis, gently over one small section of the agar surface in a zigzag pattern. Using another sterile inoculation loop, drag some

26


bacteria from the last 3-5 lines of the zigzag pattern of the first quadrant into the second quadrant. Repeat this streak process
for a third and fourth quadrant using new sterile inoculation loops for each quadrant and dragging from the previous area.
This process dilutes the bacteria over the plate to isolate single bacterial colonies.

3. Incubate the plate at 36 °C for 24 h in an aerobic atmosphere to obtain isolated and pure colonies of E. faecalis (Fig. 5) (Fig.
6a).

Incubate the plate upside down (lid down).

4. Using aseptic technique and a sterile inoculation loop, transfer isolated and pure colonies to a 13 x 100 mm tube containing
5 mL sterile BHI broth (Fig. 6b) until reaching an optical density of 1.5 in 520 nm (equivalent to 109 CFU/mL).

It is important to strictly follow the instructions of the manufacturer of the tube spectrophotometer used.

BASIC PROTOCOL 7
Basic protocol title:
SET INCUBATION
Introductory paragraph:
This protocol (basic protocol 7) describes how to incubate and maintain the sets throughout all 6 weeks of the experiment.
During the incubation process it is necessary to add sterile fresh medium inside the root canal to guarantee the presence
of nutrients and avoid drying out the medium. The use of PPE, an aseptic environment (such as biosafety cabinet or working
area of the bunsen burner), and disinfection of gloves and surfaces with 70% ethanol are important to prevent
contamination.
Materials:
70% ethanol
Enterococcosel broth medium (see recipe)
BHI broth (see recipe)

Bacteriological incubator
PPE

28


Biosafety cabinet or bunsen burner
Sterile tips
Micropipette
Sterile surface
1 mL syringe with needle
Sterile tweezers
#30 sterile endodontic paper point (TDK)

13 x 100 mm glass tubes

1. Immediately after the inoculation, incubate the set at 36 °C for 6 weeks in an aerobic atmosphere.

To avoid leakage of the inoculum to the outside of the tooth, gently open and close the incubator door (this avoids shaking the
incubated sets), and keep the sets vertically throughout the experiment. Using a rack adjusted to the diameter of the tubes
can help keep them in the vertical position.

2. Two days (48 h) after inoculation dispense carefully 20 µL of a fresh BHI broth without inoculum inside the root canal in the
most apical region.

Pipette 20 µL of BHI broth with an aseptic micropipette, dispense the content on a sterile surface and aspirate it using a 1 mL
syringe with needle. It is important to avoid air aspiration in this step.

3. Twice a week dispense carefully 20 µL of fresh sterile BHI broth inside the root canal in the most apical region.

Steps 2 and 3 ensure the viability of E. faecalis.

4. Observe all sets daily during 6 weeks to determine if and when bacterial microleakage occurred and by what pathway (Fig
7).

No bacterial microleakage results in no color change ( Fig. 7a ). A change from the bottom indicates leakage through the
obturation (Fig 7b); from the top, it demonstrates surface contamination, and the set should be discarded (Fig 7c).

5. After 6 weeks of incubation, using a sterile tweezer, insert a #30 sterile paper point ( TDK) for 1 min inside the root canals
of all sets without bacterial microleakage (Fig. 7a).

6. Transfer the paper point (TDK), using a sterile tweezer, to a 13 x 100 mm tube with 1mL enterococcosel broth.

7. Incube the tube at 36 °C for 24 h in an aerobic atmosphere.

Steps 5-7 are important to confirm the presence of viable E. faecalis inside the root canals of all sets without color changes
(Fig. 7a). Tubes without color change (Fig. 8a) indicate the absence of E. faecalis in the paper point. Whereas tubes with color
change (Fig. 8b) indicate the presence of E. faecalis in the paper point. These steps guarantee that the unchanged set color
(Fig. 7a) faithfully represents an absence of bacterial microleakage by obturation even with viable E. faecalis inside the root
canals.

COMMENTARY:
Critical Parameters:
Basic protocol 1:
When working with fresh bovine teeth, it is worth considering the anatomical diversity of the teeth, making it necessary to
have a larger quantity due to the high exclusion rate. It is important to store them in flasks with lids containing 0.9% sterile
saline. To keep the teeth hydrated, with their characteristics, and prevent dehydration, maintain the flasks refrigerated at
4°C. The use of a magnifying lens and incident light can improve the visualisation during selection of bovine teeth with
completely formed roots and without visual cracks in the roots. It's important to sharpen the Gracey periodontal curette
before removing external teeth structures (e.g: bone, calculus). This protocol should be performed by a dentist or a dental
hygienist, depending on the local legislation.
Basic protocol 2:
It is important that the digital phosphor plate is intact and that the intraoral portable X-ray and the notebook batteries are
charged. During X -rays of the bovine teeth procedure, it is important to fix the teeth in the utility wax to prevent
displacement, avoiding distortions in the radiographic images. This protocol must be performed by a trained operator.
Basic protocol 3:
For effective decoronation of a bovine tooth, always use a double sided diamond cutting disc. It is important to screw the
disc completely into the mandrel to avoid it from coming loose during use. Once the disc comes loose, it becomes useless.
Keeping the teeth hydrated during the cutting process prevents excess dust. After removing the crown, return the root to
the refrigerated saline solution.
During canal preparation, secure the bovine root in a bench vise to prevent displacement and charge endodontic electric
motor battery, allowing the operator to perform root canal preparation. Use the endodontic files according to
manufacturer instructions to avoid their fracture during preparation.
It is important to dry the outer surface of the root to close the apex with utility wax before cleansing of the root canal
systems.
To allow the operator to seal the outer surface of the root with nail polish, the use of an object such as a toothpick into the
root canal may be helpful. This object can be inserted into a surface like styrofoam until it's completely dry. To avoid possible
adhesion of nail polish to the plastic part of the surgical paper, do not use a tight surgical paper package.
It is important that procedures involving root canal be performed by a specialist in endodontics.
Basic protocol 4:
Before inserting glass pearls into the tubes, check and discard any glass pearls with a color other than clear and make sure
they are clean and dry, dark pearls may lead to false positive interpretation. A funnel -like device can be used to assist in
inserting the correct amount of pearls into the tube.
Immediately after root canal filling with the test sealer, insert it into the tube within the glass pearls and fill with agar
medium to mimic the moist environment of the oral cavity. In this step it is important to maintain the bile aesculin agar in
liquid form, in a water bath between 55° to 60°C, prior to inserting it into the tube. To carry this out, before placing the

32


flask with agar medium in the water bath, it must be completely melted. To do this, use it immediately after autoclaving
or, if it is stored at 4°C, melt it in a microwave or in a boiling water bath.
Basic protocol 5:
Before streaking E. faecalis onto BHI agar plates, ensure the plates with medium are sterile. To do so, incubate them at
36°C for up to 24 h after preparation to monitor contamination. To cool down the agar plates before inoculating with E.
faecalis, place them in an incubator after removing them from the refrigerator.
Before transferring colonies to a tube with BHI broth to prepare the inoculum, ensure the broth is sterile, incubate it at
36°C for up to 24 h after preparation to monitor contamination.
Ensure that the E. faecalis on the BHI agar plate is pure. To achieve this, it is important to streak E. faecalis to obtain isolated
bacterial colonies. Incubate the plate upside down (lid down) and, after the incubation period, carefully observe the
morphological characteristics of the colonies. A stereoscopic microscope can aid this observation.
Protocol 5 must be performed by a microbiological trained operator, using aseptic technique and sterile tools throughout

Basic protocol 6:
During inoculation, avoid allowing the inoculum to reach the surface taking the following precautions: i) when aspirating
the inoculum with the syringe needle, avoid aspirating air (bubbles can cause the inoculum to leak, during inoculation
process, on the bile aesculin agar surface); ii) carefully insert the needle into the canal, ensuring that the inoculum is gently
dispensed only into this space. iii) when removing the needle from the canal, do not rest it in its walls to avoid projecting
particles containing E. faecalis directly on the bile aesculin agar surface, iii) keep the sets vertically throughout the all
experiment. When the inoculum reaches the surface of bile aesculin agar. When the color changes, starting from the
surface, it indicates contamination (Fig. 7c).
A microbiological trained operator must perform this protocol, using aseptic technique and sterile tools during all steps.
Basic protocol 7:
During incubation, avoid allowing E. faecalis to reach the surface taking the following precautions: i) the bacteriological
incubator door should open and close smoothly, avoiding vibrations and spillage of the inoculum; ii) when adding a new
fresh medium inside the root canal, aspirate the BHI, avoi d aspirating air, ensuring that the medium is gently dispensed
only into the root canal, and do not rest the needle in the root walls when removing it from the canal; and iii) keep the sets
vertically throughout the experiment, avoiding leaks of the bacteria onto the surface of the bile aesculin agar.
When the color changes, starting from the surface, it indicates contamination (Fig. 7c). Protocol 7 must be performed using
sterile tools and aseptic technique by a microbiological trained operator.

Understanding Results:
Through visual selection and mechanical cleaning with a periodontal curette (Fig. 2 ), basic protocol 1 selects a
homogeneous group of clean bovine teeth. These selected teeth must not have external structures (e.g: bone, calculus),
nor cracks. Teeth with fully formed roots with a minimum length of 22 mm are essential for the execution of subsequent
protocols. Proper storage in sterile saline solution at 4°C ensures the preservation of the structural integrity of the
specimens until use.
Basic protocol 2, through digital radiographic evaluation, allows the identification of the anatomical characteristics of the
root canal. Teeth with multiple canals, lateral canals, and apical deltas should be excluded ( Fig. 3a-b), and included teeth
that present a single root canal (Fig. 3c), enabling the use of similar specimens in this proposed protocol. The decoronation
process, chemomechanical endodontic preparation up to #45.06, external sealing of the roots with nail polish and
autoclaving, results i n a group of sterile 22 mm bovine roots with isolated external faces and their single canals are
standardized and cleaned at the end of basic protocol 3.
Basic protocol 4 presents a preparation of sterile sets to be used in this proposed protocol. Each set is composed of a
borosilicate glass tube containing glass pearls, obturated bovine root and bile aesculin agar (Fig. 4). This basic protocol also
describes how to detect possible contamination during set preparation. Contaminated sets should be discarded.
Basic protocol 5 describes the revival of E. faecalis ATCC 2921 from a frozen stock culture. After streaking and incubation
of 36 °C for 24 h, isolated colonies should be visible away from the initial streaking area (Fig. 5). Additionally, the preparation
of an inoculum from isolated and pure E. faecalis colonies (Fig. 6a-b) containing 109 CFU per 1 mL of BHI broth is presented
in this protocol.
The methods described in basic protocols 6 and 7 allow us to obtain inoculated sets ( Fig. 6c) with 20 µL (~2x107 CFU/mL)
of E. faecalis inside the root canal, incubated vertically for 6 weeks, with addition of fresh medium inside the root canals
twice a week, and daily observed to detect changes of color of the bile aesculin agar (Fig. 7). Figure 7 represents the most
common results that can be observed in this protocol, being: i) unchanged color of the medium (bile aesculin agar), resulting
from the absence of bacterial microleakage by the endodontic sealer used to obturate the root canals ( Fig. 7a); ii) change

34


of the color of bile aesculin agar from yellow/light brown to dark brown initiated from within the medium, due to the
hydrolysis of aesculin by E. faecalis, resulting from the presence of this bacteria microleakage through the endodontic sealer
used to obturate the root canals ( Fig. 7b); iii) change in color of bile aesculin agar from yellow/light brown to dark brown,
beginning at the surface of the medium, due to aesculin hydrolysis by E. faecalis , resulting from the presence of this
bacterium on the agar surface, indicating contamination via the external root pathway; sets presenting this characteristics
should be discarded (Fig. 7c).
At the end of the assay (6 weeks), sets such as the one shown in figure 7a need to confirm the presence of viable E. faecalis
in the root canal. To do this, a sterile paper point can be inserted into the root canal and transferred to a broth that indicates
presence of E. faecalis. After the incubation period, the esculetin, resulting from the hydrolysis of aesculin, reacts with ferric
ions present in the medium, such as enterococcosel broth, forming a dark complex ( Fig. 8b), while in the absence of the
microorganisms that caused this reaction, the medium maintains its original color (Fig. 8a).
Figures 9 and 10 show different concentrations of E. faecalis over time inoculated either inside the root canal without
obturation or externally to the root, respectively. The concentration of the inoculum is inversely proportional to the time
required for the medium to change color, regardless of where the inoculat ion occurs. Comparing these figures, there is a
clear difference when E. faecalis reaches the culture medium through the root canal ( Fig. 9 - color is first seen and
disseminates from the bottom upward) or through contamination on its surface ( Fig.10 - color is first seen at the top and
spreads down), regardless of the inoculum concentration. So, the tubes contaminated on the surface can be easily identified
during daily visual inspection.

Time Considerations:
The entire protocol can be completed in approximately 8 to 9 weeks, but depending on slaughterhouse availability as well
as of the number of roots tested, the period can be considerably extended.
The selection and cleaning of bovine teeth (basic protocol 1) takes 1 day. Basic protocol 2 takes 1 day to take and analyze
the radiographs, applying the inclusion criteria. The preparation of the teeth included in the study (basic protocol 3) is the
most laborious phase of teeth preparation (basic protocol 1-3). It begins with the decoration of the bovine teeth, which
takes 1 to 2 days, while the standardization of the cervical, middle, and apical thirds of the teeth can be performed in 1 to
2 days. Root canal cleaning takes 1 day, but an additional day (for complete drying) is required before performing the
next step. Sealing the tooth with enamel takes 2 days. Basic protocol 4 needs about 2-3 days to prepare the sets
containing glass pearls, bovine root with its canal filled with endodontic sealer, requiring an extra day before inoculating
them. Inoculum preparation (basic protocol 5) and canal inoculation (basic protocol 6), require 2 days to prepare the
media, streak the E. faecalis, prepare the inoculum and perform the inoculation. Basic protocol 7 (set incubation) requires
daily observation for 6 weeks, with addition of fresh medium inside root canals twice a week.

4 CONSIDERAÇÕES GERAIS


Diante do exposto, conclui -se que a microinfiltração endodôntica representa um
desafio persistente à previsibilidade e longevidade dos tratamentos endodônticos. A
complexidade anatômica do sistema de canais radiculares, aliada à resistência microbiana,
especialmente de biofilmes formados por Enterococcus faecalis e Candida albicans ,
compromete a eficácia da limpeza e do selamento do SCR. Embora os cimentos
endodônticos atuais reúnam propriedades físico-químicas e biológicas desejáveis, sua ação
ainda demanda avaliações contínuas por meio de modelos experimentais, sendo assim a
adoção de protocolos laboratoriais, como os testes de microinfiltração microbiana,
contribuem para o aprimoramento da avaliação dos materiais obturadores.
O avanço na compreensão da microinfiltração microbiana e na seleção de materiais
obturadores, a partir dos ensaios laboratoriais, com maior capacidade de vedação é
fundamental para reduzir a taxa de insucesso terapêutico e promover a excelência na
prática endodôntica.

RESUMO

O tratamento endodôntico visa reduzir ao máximo a carga microbiana presente no
sistema de canais radiculares por meio do preparo químico -mecânico, utilizando
instrumentos manuais e/ou mecanizados sob ação de substâncias irrigadoras. Para evitar
o fracasso do tratamento endodôntico, é importante selar adequadamente os canais após
o preparo químico -mecânico, a fim de evitar microinfiltração microbiana. O selamento
envolve o uso de guta -percha e cimento endodôntico, este último aderindo à dentina e
preenchendo os espaços entre a guta-percha e o sistema de canais radiculares, entretanto
falhas na integridade e limitações dos materiais obturadores e restauradores podem
predispor a microinfiltração. Com o objetivo de se entender melhor a microinfiltração,
estudos laboratoriais apresentam diversos tipos de análise em materiais obturadores. Entre
os modelos, destaca -se o método de duas câmaras para avaliar a infiltração microbiana,
contudo não garante que esta microinfiltração ocorre através do espaço do canal radicular
e não por outras vias. O objetivo deste estudo foi desenvolver um protocolo laboratorial para
avaliar a microinfiltração microbiana através dos cimentos endodônticos, de forma a garantir
a visualização da via de infiltração do inóculo. Para tanto, foi desenvolvido um sistema
contendo raízes de dentes bovinos, tubos de vidro com pérolas de vidro e meio de cultura
ágar bile esculina. Cada raiz, após preparo, desinfecção e ester ilização em autoclave, foi
inserida em um tubo estéril de vidro contendo pérolas de vidro, previamente pesadas, este
conjunto foi parcialmente preenchido com meio ágar bile esculina e sua esterilidade
verificada pela incubação por 24 h. Após este período, o sistema foi inoculado com
Enterococcus faecalis ATCC 29212, incubado a 36°C e observado por 6 semanas. O ensaio
laboratorial proposto permitiu detectar se a infiltração por E. faecalis ocorreu via canal
radicular ou externamente a raiz devido a alteração da coloração por oxidação do meio de
cultura; na região apical através do seu longo eixo do canal radicular ou superficialmente
ao meio de cultura quando, por falha do operador, alguma quantidade do inóculo seja
depositado externamente à raiz. Conclui -se que este novo protocolo apresenta as
características necessárias para avaliar microinfiltração microbiana através dos cimentos
endodônticos, visto sua capacidade de demonstrar a via da microinfiltração, garantindo
diferenciar microinfiltração de contaminação.

Palavras-chave: bactéria; microbiologia; endodontia; infiltração dentária; protocolo.

ABSTRACT

Endodontic treatment aims to reduce as much as possible the microbial load present in the
root canal system through chemical -mechanical preparation, using manual and/or
mechanized instruments under the action of irrigating substances. To avoid the failure of
endodontic treatment, it is important to adequately seal the canals after chemical -
mechanical preparation, to prevent microbial microleakage. The sealing involves the use of
gutta-percha and endodontic cement, the latter adhering to dentin and filling t he spaces
between the gutta-percha and the dentin walls; however, failures in integrity and limitations
of obturating and restorative materials may predispose to microleakage. With the objective
of better understanding microleakage, laboratory studies pres ent several types of analysis
in obturating materials. Among the models, the two -chamber method stands out for
evaluating microbial leakage; however, it does not guarantee that this microleakage occurs
through the root canal space and not by other pathways. The objective of this study was to
develop a laboratory protocol to evaluate microbial microleakage through endodontic
sealers, in order to ensure visualization of the inoculum leakage pathway. For this purpose,
a system was developed containing bovine tooth roots, glass tubes with glass beads, and
bile esculin agar culture medium. Each root, after preparation, disinfection, and sterilization
in autoclave, was inserted into a sterile glass tube containing previously weighed glass
beads; this set was partially filled with bile esculin agar medium and its sterility verified by
incubation for 24 h. After this period, the system was inoculated with Enterococcus faecalis
ATCC 29212, incubated at 36°C, and observed for 6 weeks. The proposed laboratory assay
allowed detection of whether infiltration by E. faecalis occurred via the root canal or
externally to the root due to color change by oxidation of the culture medium; in the apical
region through the long axis of the root canal or superficially to the culture medium when,
due to operator failure, some amount of the inoculum was deposited externally to the root.
It is concluded that thi s new protocol presents the necessary characteristics to evaluate
microbial microleakage through endodontic cements, given its ability to demonstrate the
pathway of microleakage, ensuring differentiation between microleakage and
contamination.

1 INTRODUÇÃO


A perda da integridade das estruturas dentárias favorece a penetração de
microrganismos no sistema de canais radiculares (SCR). Esse evento ocorre quando
estruturas dentárias, como o esmalte ou cemento, que compõem a parte externa do dente,
e a dentina, que representa a maior parte da estrutura dentária, sofrem ruptura por fatores
biológicos ou traumáticos (Farci; Soni, 2023). O estudo clássico de Kakehashi , Stanley e
Fitzgerald (1965), demonstrou que a presença de microrganismos é determinante para o
desenvolvimento de lesões periapicais, o que foi corroborado por estudos mais recentes
(Aw, 2016; Farci; Soni, 2023; Nair, 2004).
Dentre os microrganismos frequentemente associados à infecção endodôntica
destacam-se Enterococcus faecalis e Candida albicans (Ajmi et al., 2024), que possuem a
capacidade de formar biofilmes, conferindo -lhes resistência aos processos de limpeza do
SCR, elevando o risco de falha no tratamento endodôntico (Siqueira Jr; Rôças, 2008).
Particularmente, E. faecalis destaca-se por sua resistência aos antimicrobianos
convencionais e pela habilidade de sobreviver em condições desfavoráveis dentro do SCR
(Sharma et al., 2025). A complexa estrutura dos canais radiculares, incluindo istmos e
canais laterais, se tornam nichos para a sobrevivência microbiana, dificultando a limpeza
química e mecânica (Ajmi et al., 2024; Martins et al., 2019; Prada et al., 2019; Sharma et
al., 2025; Siqueira Jr; Rôças, 2008).
Nesse contexto, o tratamento endodôntico visa reduzir ao máximo a carga
microbiana presente no SCR por meio do preparo químico -mecânico (PQM), utilizando
instrumentos manuais e/ou mecanizados sob ação de substâncias irrigadoras, como
hipoclorito de sódio ( Haapasalo et al., 2010), e obturação com materiais biocompatíveis
(Gatelli; Bortolini, 2014; Macedo et al., 2021; Schilder, 2006; Vier et al., 2011).
A guta-percha, que atua como material obturador, apresenta ação limitada, e não é
capaz, isoladamente, de garantir um selamento duradouro (Schilder, 2006). Dessa forma,
a utilização de cimentos endodônticos, pode contribuir para a melhora desse selamento
(Komabayashi et al., 2020; Kowalski et al., 2024). Sendo assim, a guta -percha associada
aos cimentos endodônticos buscam preencher de forma tridimensional o SCR, auxiliando
na prevenção de futuras infecções (Hori et al., 2021; Siqueira Jr.; Roças; 2008).

12


Evitar a microinfiltração microbiana, através da obturação, é essencial para
aumentar a eficácia, a previsibilidade e o sucesso dos procedimentos endodônticos (Ajmi
et al., 2024; Jafari et al., 2017). Contudo, falhas na integridade e limitações dos materiais
obturadores e restauradores podem resultar em microinfiltração (Ajmi et al., 2024; Jafari;
Jafari, 2017; Wuersching et al., 2023).
Para que sejam considerados ideais, os cimentos endodônticos devem reunir
propriedades que garantam excelente selamento e compatibilidade biológica com os
tecidos periapicais (Rekha et al., 2023). Esses cimentos podem apresentar características
como: biocompatibilidade, selamento eficaz, ação antimicrobiana, estabilidade em meio
úmido, radiopacidade, boa adesão ao canal radicular, tempo de trabalho prolongado e
ausência de contração durante a presa (Bran stetter; Von Fraunhofer, 1982), e podem
apresentar em sua composição: óxido de zinco -eugenol, salicilato, óxido de zinco -ácido
graxo, ionômero de vidro, silicone, resina epóxi, silicato tricálcico (agregado de trióxido
mineral MTA/biocerâmica) e resina de metacrilato (Komabayashi et al., 2020).
Ainda que sejam encontrados cimentos endodônticos com as propriedades
descritas anteriormente, tem -se observado o insucesso dos tratamentos endodônticos
devido à microinfiltração microbiana, resultando em uma infecção endodôntica secundária
(D'costa; Bangera; Kutty, 2017; Khayat; Lee; Torabinejad, 1993; Roghanizad; Jones, 1996;
Swanson; Madison, 1987).
É importante realizar pesquisas laboratoriais que verifiquem a microinfiltração
através dos cimentos endodônticos já utilizados, bem como também de novos (Akhavan et
al., 2011; Jafari; Jafari, 2017; Jafari et al ., 2017). Assim sendo, estudos apresentam
diferentes metodologias para verificar a microinfiltração, como, por infiltração de glicose,
com corantes como o azul de metileno, por pressão de fluidos no corpo de prova (calculado
a partir do movimento da bolha) e também microinfiltração bacteriana; com o intuito de
qualificar o selamento dos condutos radiculares (Akhavan et al., 2011; Jafari; Jafari, 2017;
Jafari et al., 2017). Dentre os modelos para verificar microinfiltração microbiana, destaca -
se o método que utiliza um sistema de duas câmaras. A câmara superior é composta por
um microtubo adaptado, contendo raízes dentárias previamente preparadas e seladas com
esmalte de unha e cianoacrilato. Após esterilização com óxido de etileno, essa câmera é
acoplada à inferior (um frasco de vidro contendo meio de cultura líquido estéril). A
extremidade da raiz permanece submersa no meio, sem tocar o fundo do frasco. A turvação

13


do meio de cultura indica ocorrência de microinfiltração bacteriana (Mansour et al., 2024;
Shahi et al., 2017; Yanpiset et al., 2018).
No entanto, revisões de literatura apontam limitações nos estudos de
microinfiltração microbiana com duas câmaras (Jafari; Jafari, 2017; Rechenberg; De-Deus;
Zehnder, 2011), como o uso do cianoacrilato como material selante, onde a microinfiltração
pode ocorrer na interface dente -tubo da câmara superior e não pelo espaço do canal
radicular (Jafari et al., 2017).
Embora muitos dos estudos que avaliaram microinfiltração tenham utilizado dentes
humanos (Jafari et al., 2017; Jafari; Jafari, 2017; Kim et al., 2015; Komabayashi et al., 2020;
Moradi et al., 2009; Rechenberg; De-Deus; Zehnder, 2011; Rekha et al., 2023; Wuersching
et al., 2023), a substituição por dentes bovinos em estudos de endodontia tem se mostrado
eficaz (Azevedo et al., 2025; Brackett et al., 1998; Carvalho et al., 2018; Schmalz et al.,
2001; Silva et al., 2019; Yassen; Platt; Hara, 2011). Mesmo con siderando que a dentina
bovina apresenta maior permeabilidade, essa diferença é pequena, uma vez que o número
e diâmetro de túbulos são semelhantes às da dentina humana, porém com maior densidade
(Schilke et al., 2000), sendo os dentes bovinos considerados uma alternativa viável para
testes de permeabilidade e resistência de união em obturação com guta -percha e cimento
(Carvalho et al., 2018; Silva et al., 2019). Adicionalmente, a utilização desses dentes em
ensaios laboratoriais apresenta como vantagem a m aior facilidade de obtenção em
comparação aos dentes humanos (Schmalz et al., 2001), cuja disponibilidade é limitada
(Tanaka et al., 2008).
Uma vez que o selamento eficaz do SCR está associado ao sucesso do tratamento
endodôntico e os métodos de avaliação da microinfiltração microbiana são questionados
por não garantirem que a via de acesso do microrganismo ao meio de cultura ocorreu
através da obturação, t orna-se importante o desenvolvimento de um novo modelo
experimental que permita avaliar com precisão a infiltração microbiana em raízes obturadas
com diferentes materiais obturadores.

ABSTRACT:
To avoid failure of endodontic treatment, it is important to properly seal the canals after chemomechanical preparation, in o rder to
avoid microleakage. Typically, sealing involves the use of gutta-percha and sealing cement, the latter of which adheres to the dentin
and fills the spaces between the gutta-percha and the dentin walls. Laboratory studies have been performed to detect microleakage
of endodontic sealers based on various criteria, including microbiological ones, however none guarantee that the le akage occurred
through the root canal space and not through other pathways. Our protocols propose a new laboratory assay to evaluate bacteri al
microleakage in endodontic sealers, ensuring visualization of the correct inoculum infiltration pathway. Furthermore, we present the
main critical parameters and provide suggestions on how to manage them. These protocols allow the detection of bacterial
microleakage in bovine teeth filled with endodontic sealer and inoculated with Enterococcus faecalis.

INTRODUCTION:
The tooth has two main parts, crown and root, being externally covered by enamel and cement, respectively. Internally, it
is composed of dentin and dental pulp ( Farci & Soni, 2023 ). Endodontic infection occurs mainly due to the exposure of the dental
pulp to the oral cavity (Nair, 2004), and the presence of microorganisms in the root canal system triggers an inflammatory response
resulting in apical periodontitis (Aw, 2016; Kakerashi et al., 1965; Nair, 2004 ).
The success of endodontic treatment in teeth with apical periodontitis is associated with reducing the bacterial load to
levels compatible with healing ( Siqueria & Roças, 2008 ). This treatment relies on a chemomechanical approach, which combines
instrumentation and irrigation procedures for achieving effective cleansing of the root canal system ( Byström et al., 1987; Garcez et
al., 2007). To avoid endodontic treatment failure it is also important to properly seal the canals after chemomechanical preparation,
in order to prevent microleakage (Deshpande & Naik, 2015; Jafari & Jafari, 2017, Komabayashi et al., 2020; Muliyar et al., 2014,).

17


Typically, sealing involves the use of gutta-percha, a semi-solid material, and sealing cement. Gutta-percha acts as a filling
material, while endodontic cement adheres to the dentin and fills spaces between gutta -percha and the dentinal walls ( Muliyar et
al., 2014).
Endodontic sealers are classified by composition as: zinc oxide -eugenol, salicylate, zinc oxide -fatty acid, glass ionomer,
silicone, epoxy resin, tricalcium silicate ( MTA Mineral Trioxide Aggregate /bioceramic), and methacrylate resin ( Komabayashi et al.,
2020). Currently, different laboratory studies have been performed for detecting microleakage of endodontic sealers, based on: dye
penetration, dye extraction, fluid filtration, glucose penetration, bacterial leakage, endotoxin infiltration, caffeine pene tration,
caffeine microleakage, protein penetration, copper ion diffusion, radioisotope penetration, and electrochemical leakage tests (Jafari
& Jafari, 2017; Komabayashi et al ., 2020 ). Review studies have presented limitations and disadvantages associated with these
methodologies (Jafari & Jafari 2017; Rechenberg et al., 2010; Verissimo & Do Vale, 2006 ), especially regarding microbial leakage in
two-chamber models. The main limitation they report is that this model does not guarantee that the leakage actually occurred
through the root canal space pathways and not through other pathways (Rechenberg et al., 2010).
Our study brings a novel laboratory assay to evaluate the bacterial microleakage of endodontic sealers ( Fig. 1), ensuring
visualization of the correct inoculum leakage pathway. This will allow identification of whether or not the leakage is occurring through
the root canal space. We describe the selection and cleaning of bovine teeth in basic protocol 1. Basic protocol 2 presents the inclusion
criteria and storage of the teeth. Once teeth are included, the decoronation process and standardization of shape and size of the root
canals are described in basic protocol 3, whereas basic protocol 4 provides the preparatio n of a set containing the tooth to be
inoculated. The inoculum preparation and the set inoculation with Enterococcus faecalis are described in basic protocol 5 and 6,
respectively. Basic protocol 7 demonstrates how to incubate and maintain the sets throughout all 6 weeks of experiment.

BASIC PROTOCOL 1
Basic protocol title:
BOVINE TEETH SELECTION AND CLEANING
Introductory paragraph:
This protocol describes a method to select bovine teeth by visual inspection and then clean them using a periodontal
curette. It is important to use PPE to protect the operator from contamination. This protocol allows the selection of clean
bovine teeth with completely formed roots and root size of at least 22 mm.
Materials:
Fresh bovine teeth
0.9% sterile saline (see recipe)

Gloves
Ruler
Face shield
Periodontal Gracey curette (Golgran-Millennium, São Caetano do Sul, SP, Brazil)
Plastic flasks with lid
Refrigerator

Visual evaluation
1. Obtain fresh bovine teeth from a slaughterhouse after the animal has been slaughtered (a routine activity in the
commercialization of meat for nutritional purposes).

The Brazilian Council for the Control of Animal Experimentation, as well as IACUC (Institutional Animal Care and Use
Committee), only evaluate the use of live animals in research or animals that have been euthanized for research purposes,
which was not the case in this protocol, so ethical approval is not applicable in this case.

2. Wear gloves to avoid contamination.

Fresh bovine teeth routinely come with biological materials, such as bone and gum debris, hence the need for protection with
gloves when handling these teeth.

3. Perform visual inspection.

It is necessary to be in a well-lit environment to assure visual acuity.

4. Select bovine teeth with completely formed roots.

5. Select bovine teeth that have roots with at least 22 mm (Fig. 2).

6. Select bovine teeth without cracks in the roots.

Cleaning

7. Wear a face shield to protect the operator's face.

The face shield is necessary to protect the face against the detachment of bone fragments and calculus from the bovine teeth
during the cleaning process.

8. Remove any external teeth structures, such as bone and calculus (Fig. 2a), using a periodontal Gracey curette ( Golgran-
Millennium).

9. Store clean teeth in 0.9% sterile saline solution in a plastic flask with lid in a refrigerator at 4 oC.

Replace the sterile saline solution once a week.

Use an endodontic ruler and a permanent marker to trace a 22 mm distance from the apical region to the cervical region of

Basic protocol title:
INOCULUM PREPARATION
Introductory paragraph:
This protocol describes how to obtain an inoculum with 10 9 Colony Forming Units (CFU)/mL of E. faecalis American Type
Culture Collection (ATCC) 29212, from a frozen glycerol stock, in Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) broth. To avoid contamination
rigorous aseptic techniques are necessary in all steps of basic protocol 5. For example, perform all steps wearing PPE in an
aseptic environment such as a biosafety cabinet or working area of the bunsen burner, and disinfect gloves and surfaces
with 70% ethanol.

E. faecalis ATCC 29212 frozen stock in BHI broth with glycerol (at final concentration of 20% vol./vol. glycerol)

1. Using aseptic technique remove a small chunk of frozen E. faecalis from the cryotube, using a sterile inoculating loop.

2. Streak E. faecalis onto the BHI agar plate.

Starting from the edge of the Petri dish, in the first quadrant using the sterile inoculation loop streak the small chunk of E.
faecalis, gently over one small section of the agar surface in a zigzag pattern. Using another sterile inoculation loop, drag some

bacteria from the last 3-5 lines of the zigzag pattern of the first quadrant into the second quadrant. Repeat this streak process
for a third and fourth quadrant using new sterile inoculation loops for each quadrant and dragging from the previous area.
This process dilutes the bacteria over the plate to isolate single bacterial colonies.

3. Incubate the plate at 36 °C for 24 h in an aerobic atmosphere to obtain isolated and pure colonies of E. faecalis (Fig. 5) (Fig.

4. Using aseptic technique and a sterile inoculation loop, transfer isolated and pure colonies to a 13 x 100 mm tube containing

BASIC PROTOCOL 7
Basic protocol title:
SET INCUBATION
Introductory paragraph:
This protocol (basic protocol 7) describes how to incubate and maintain the sets throughout all 6 weeks of the experiment.
During the incubation process it is necessary to add sterile fresh medium inside the root canal to guarantee the presence
of nutrients and avoid drying out the medium. The use of PPE, an aseptic environment (such as biosafety cabinet or working
area of the bunsen burner), and disinfection of gloves and surfaces with 70% ethanol are important to prevent
contamination.
Materials:
70% ethanol
Enterococcosel broth medium (see recipe)
BHI broth (see recipe)

Bacteriological incubator
PPE

28


Biosafety cabinet or bunsen burner
Sterile tips
Micropipette
Sterile surface
1 mL syringe with needle
Sterile tweezers
#30 sterile endodontic paper point (TDK)

13 x 100 mm glass tubes

1. Immediately after the inoculation, incubate the set at 36 °C for 6 weeks in an aerobic atmosphere.

To avoid leakage of the inoculum to the outside of the tooth, gently open and close the incubator door (this avoids shaking the
incubated sets), and keep the sets vertically throughout the experiment. Using a rack adjusted to the diameter of the tubes
can help keep them in the vertical position.

2. Two days (48 h) after inoculation dispense carefully 20 µL of a fresh BHI broth without inoculum inside the root canal in the
most apical region.

Pipette 20 µL of BHI broth with an aseptic micropipette, dispense the content on a sterile surface and aspirate it using a 1 mL
syringe with needle. It is important to avoid air aspiration in this step.

3. Twice a week dispense carefully 20 µL of fresh sterile BHI broth inside the root canal in the most apical region.

Steps 2 and 3 ensure the viability of E. faecalis.

4. Observe all sets daily during 6 weeks to determine if and when bacterial microleakage occurred and by what pathway (Fig
7).

No bacterial microleakage results in no color change ( Fig. 7a ). A change from the bottom indicates leakage through the
obturation (Fig 7b); from the top, it demonstrates surface contamination, and the set should be discarded (Fig 7c).

5. After 6 weeks of incubation, using a sterile tweezer, insert a #30 sterile paper point ( TDK) for 1 min inside the root canals
of all sets without bacterial microleakage (Fig. 7a).

6. Transfer the paper point (TDK), using a sterile tweezer, to a 13 x 100 mm tube with 1mL enterococcosel broth.

7. Incube the tube at 36 °C for 24 h in an aerobic atmosphere.

Steps 5-7 are important to confirm the presence of viable E. faecalis inside the root canals of all sets without color changes
(Fig. 7a). Tubes without color change (Fig. 8a) indicate the absence of E. faecalis in the paper point. Whereas tubes with color
change (Fig. 8b) indicate the presence of E. faecalis in the paper point. These steps guarantee that the unchanged set color
(Fig. 7a) faithfully represents an absence of bacterial microleakage by obturation even with viable E. faecalis inside the root
canals.

COMMENTARY:
Critical Parameters:
Basic protocol 1:
When working with fresh bovine teeth, it is worth considering the anatomical diversity of the teeth, making it necessary to
have a larger quantity due to the high exclusion rate. It is important to store them in flasks with lids containing 0.9% sterile
saline. To keep the teeth hydrated, with their characteristics, and prevent dehydration, maintain the flasks refrigerated at
4°C. The use of a magnifying lens and incident light can improve the visualisation during selection of bovine teeth with
completely formed roots and without visual cracks in the roots. It's important to sharpen the Gracey periodontal curette
before removing external teeth structures (e.g: bone, calculus). This protocol should be performed by a dentist or a dental
hygienist, depending on the local legislation.
Basic protocol 2:
It is important that the digital phosphor plate is intact and that the intraoral portable X-ray and the notebook batteries are
charged. During X -rays of the bovine teeth procedure, it is important to fix the teeth in the utility wax to prevent
displacement, avoiding distortions in the radiographic images. This protocol must be performed by a trained operator.
Basic protocol 3:
For effective decoronation of a bovine tooth, always use a double sided diamond cutting disc. It is important to screw the
disc completely into the mandrel to avoid it from coming loose during use. Once the disc comes loose, it becomes useless.
Keeping the teeth hydrated during the cutting process prevents excess dust. After removing the crown, return the root to
the refrigerated saline solution.
During canal preparation, secure the bovine root in a bench vise to prevent displacement and charge endodontic electric
motor battery, allowing the operator to perform root canal preparation. Use the endodontic files according to
manufacturer instructions to avoid their fracture during preparation.
It is important to dry the outer surface of the root to close the apex with utility wax before cleansing of the root canal
systems.
To allow the operator to seal the outer surface of the root with nail polish, the use of an object such as a toothpick into the
root canal may be helpful. This object can be inserted into a surface like styrofoam until it's completely dry. To avoid possible
adhesion of nail polish to the plastic part of the surgical paper, do not use a tight surgical paper package.
It is important that procedures involving root canal be performed by a specialist in endodontics.
Basic protocol 4:
Before inserting glass pearls into the tubes, check and discard any glass pearls with a color other than clear and make sure
they are clean and dry, dark pearls may lead to false positive interpretation. A funnel -like device can be used to assist in
inserting the correct amount of pearls into the tube.
Immediately after root canal filling with the test sealer, insert it into the tube within the glass pearls and fill with agar
medium to mimic the moist environment of the oral cavity. In this step it is important to maintain the bile aesculin agar in
liquid form, in a water bath between 55° to 60°C, prior to inserting it into the tube. To carry this out, before placing the

32


flask with agar medium in the water bath, it must be completely melted. To do this, use it immediately after autoclaving
or, if it is stored at 4°C, melt it in a microwave or in a boiling water bath.
Basic protocol 5:
Before streaking E. faecalis onto BHI agar plates, ensure the plates with medium are sterile. To do so, incubate them at
36°C for up to 24 h after preparation to monitor contamination. To cool down the agar plates before inoculating with E.
faecalis, place them in an incubator after removing them from the refrigerator.
Before transferring colonies to a tube with BHI broth to prepare the inoculum, ensure the broth is sterile, incubate it at
36°C for up to 24 h after preparation to monitor contamination.
Ensure that the E. faecalis on the BHI agar plate is pure. To achieve this, it is important to streak E. faecalis to obtain isolated
bacterial colonies. Incubate the plate upside down (lid down) and, after the incubation period, carefully observe the
morphological characteristics of the colonies. A stereoscopic microscope can aid this observation.
Protocol 5 must be performed by a microbiological trained operator, using aseptic technique and sterile tools throughout
this protocol.
Basic protocol 6:
During inoculation, avoid allowing the inoculum to reach the surface taking the following precautions: i) when aspirating
the inoculum with the syringe needle, avoid aspirating air (bubbles can cause the inoculum to leak, during inoculation
process, on the bile aesculin agar surface); ii) carefully insert the needle into the canal, ensuring that the inoculum is gently
dispensed only into this space. iii) when removing the needle from the canal, do not rest it in its walls to avoid projecting
particles containing E. faecalis directly on the bile aesculin agar surface, iii) keep the sets vertically throughout the all
experiment. When the inoculum reaches the surface of bile aesculin agar. When the color changes, starting from the
surface, it indicates contamination (Fig. 7c).
A microbiological trained operator must perform this protocol, using aseptic technique and sterile tools during all steps.
Basic protocol 7:
During incubation, avoid allowing E. faecalis to reach the surface taking the following precautions: i) the bacteriological
incubator door should open and close smoothly, avoiding vibrations and spillage of the inoculum; ii) when adding a new
fresh medium inside the root canal, aspirate the BHI, avoi d aspirating air, ensuring that the medium is gently dispensed
only into the root canal, and do not rest the needle in the root walls when removing it from the canal; and iii) keep the sets

When the color changes, starting from the surface, it indicates contamination (Fig. 7c). Protocol 7 must be performed using
